titre: The Restoration That Saved a Village
accroche: An 81-year-old parishioner retouches a fresco of Christ while it dries. The result goes around the world and draws 150,000 visitors.
contenu_vulgarise:
Around 1930, the painter Elías García Martínez paints directly on the wall of the church of the Sanctuary of Mercy in Borja, in northern Spain, a small fresco of Christ crowned with thorns: an *Ecce Homo* measuring 50 by 40 centimeters, given to a village where he spent his vacations. The work, press accounts unanimously say, is nothing remarkable artistically. The dampness of the wall, however, seriously damages it over the decades, to the point that part of the paint flakes off.

In 2012, Cecilia Giménez, an 81-year-old parishioner and untrained amateur painter, sets out to restore it herself, with the agreement of the parish priest. “The priest knew it. I've never tried to do anything hidden,” she would later say on Spanish television. She leaves her work to dry, unfinished by her own account, and goes on vacation for two weeks, thinking she will finish it when she returns.

## The Turning Point

When she gets back, the affair has gone around the world. Photographs of the repainted face, with thickened features and fur suggested by imprecise brushstrokes, circulate online under the name *Ecce Mono*, “behold the monkey.” A BBC correspondent describes the result as “a pencil sketch of a very hairy monkey in an ill-fitting tunic.” The original painter's family threatens legal action, the priest briefly considers covering the fresco, and Giménez, overwhelmed by the attention, loses six kilos in a few weeks, refusing to eat.

The reversal follows hard on the heels of the humiliation. The village, until then ignored by tourist maps, sees 150,000 visitors flock in to see with their own eyes the painting that has become a global phenomenon. An interpretation center devoted to the affair opens in 2016, with multilingual signs and merchandise. The fresco itself has never been restored a second time.

## What It Shifts

Giménez herself would eventually come to see her act differently. “Everyone here now sees what I did in a different light,” she said in 2015. “This restoration put Borja on the world map, which means I did something for my village that no one else had managed to do.” The episode proves nothing about the quality of a failed restoration. It does show, however, how far the value attributed to a work can shift entirely, without a single additional brushstroke being responsible: it is no longer García Martínez's fresco that the world comes to see in Borja, it is Cecilia Giménez's.

carte.punch: A botched restoration becomes the tourist attraction of an entire village.
carte.idee: In 2012, an 81-year-old parishioner single-handedly retouches a fresco of Christ in a Spanish church. The result, nicknamed Ecce Mono, becomes a global phenomenon. The village draws 150,000 visitors, and a center is dedicated to it in 2016.

quiz.question: According to the entry, what turns the Borja fresco affair from a local incident into a worldwide episode?
choix: An official complaint filed by the Diocese of Tarazona against Cecilia Giménez
The worldwide spread online of photographs of the retouched fresco, compared to a monkey
The village's announcement of a fundraising drive to pay for a new restoration
The priest's decision to close the church to the public during the investigation
quiz.explication: It is the circulation of photographs of the repainted face, nicknamed Ecce Mono and compared to a monkey by the international press, that tips the affair from a parish incident into a worldwide phenomenon. Neither a complaint from the diocese, nor a fundraising drive, nor a closing of the church appears in the sequence of events.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what circumstances does Cecilia Giménez set out to restore the fresco in 2012?
choix: In secret, without telling anyone in the parish, at night
On commission from the diocese, which had budgeted for a professional restoration
On her own initiative, with the priest's agreement, as a parishioner and amateur painter
After a call for volunteers issued by the Borja town hall
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cecilia Giménez, an 81-year-old parishioner and untrained amateur painter, undertakes the restoration on her own with the priest's agreement, as she herself would confirm: the priest knew.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What physical and personal consequences does Cecilia Giménez suffer when the affair goes global?
choix: She is briefly hospitalized after a fall in the church
She loses six kilos in a few weeks and refuses to eat
She leaves the village for good to escape the media attention
She is charged by the Spanish courts for damaging religious property
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Overwhelmed by the media attention, Cecilia Giménez loses six kilos in a few weeks and refuses to eat, before the affair turns in the village's favor.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the village of Borja open in 2016 to welcome visitors who come to see the fresco?
choix: A sacred art museum devoted exclusively to García Martínez's original work
An official online shop selling digital reproductions of the fresco
A second church, built to relieve crowding at the Sanctuary of Mercy
An interpretation center, with multilingual signs and merchandise
quiz_supplementaire.explication: An interpretation center devoted to the affair opens in 2016, with multilingual signs and merchandise, a sign of the tourist scale the episode has taken on.
